passages.t: The Day will come like a thief
passages.happening:
“Now about the times and seasons, brothers, we do not need to write to you. For you are fully aware that the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (verses 1-2).

“While people are saying, ‘Peace and security,’ destruction will come upon them suddenly, like labor pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
After telling them that the dead in Christ will rise, Paul turns to the next question the church seems to have had: when? ‘Times and seasons’ means dates and periods. Paul's answer is that they already know. They know that no one knows.

‘The Day of the Lord’ was the prophets' name for the day when God would step in to judge evil and save his people. Paul now ties it to the coming of Jesus. And he uses a picture that goes back to Jesus himself: a thief in the night. A thief does not send word ahead. The point is not that the Day is sneaky, but that it is sudden. It will come when people are not looking for it.

The people who will be caught are those saying ‘Peace and security’. Many scholars hear in those words the boasts of Rome, which praised the peace and safety its rule had brought to the world on its coins and inscriptions. Others hear the false prophets of Jeremiah's day, who said all was well when it was not. Either way, it is the confidence of people who feel safe without God.

The second picture is labour pains. They come suddenly, and once they start there is no stopping them. But labour pains also mean that a birth is near. The Day of the Lord is judgment, and it is also the start of something new.
passages.ot:
The prophets warned about the Day of the LORD. Amos told those who longed for it, “What will the Day of the LORD be for you? It will be darkness and not light” (Amos 5:18). Isaiah said, “Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near” and that on that day people “will writhe like a woman in labor” (Isaiah 13:6, 8).

Jeremiah condemned prophets who comforted people falsely, “saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace at all” (Jeremiah 6:14).
passages.hard:
If the Day comes like a thief, can anyone work out when it will be?

No, and Paul does not try. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36). After his resurrection he told his disciples, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority” (Acts 1:7).

Many people over the centuries have set dates for the Lord's return, and every one has come and gone. Some have claimed that a particular war, leader, nation or event of their own time was the sign these verses speak of. Those claims go beyond what Paul wrote, and they have often frightened people, divided churches and damaged faith. These notes set no date and name no event.

What Paul gives instead is a way of living. That is what the next verses are about.
passages.asks: Paul says the Day will come when people feel most secure. Ask where you feel safe without God, in your money, your health, your plans or your country. Ask whether you are more curious about when the Lord will come than about whether you are ready. And ask what you would want to be doing if he came today.

passages.t: Children of the day: awake, sober, and armed with faith, love and hope
passages.happening:
“But you, brothers, are not in the darkness so that this day should overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of the light and sons of the day; we do not belong to the night or to the darkness” (verses 4-5).

“So then, let us not sleep as the others do, but let us remain awake and sober” (verse 6). “But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation. For God has not appointed us to suffer wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him” (verses 8-10).

“Therefore encourage and build one another up, just as you are already doing” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Paul does not tell them the date. He tells them who they are. They are ‘sons of the light and sons of the day’, a Hebrew way of saying that they belong to the light. The Day will not catch them off guard, not because they know when it will come, but because they are already awake.

Night in an ancient city was very dark. There were no street lights and no police. Night was when people got drunk, when thieves broke in, when people did what they did not want seen. Paul uses all of that. Believers are not to sleep, meaning not to drift through life careless of God. They are to stay sober, meaning clear-headed and alert.

Then he dresses them for the watch. A breastplate guards the heart; a helmet guards the head. The breastplate is made of faith and love, and the helmet of hope. Those are the three words Paul thanked God for at the start of the letter (1:3). The Christian's armour is not weapons. It is trust in God, love for others, and hope.

Verse 9 gives the ground of that hope. God has ‘appointed’ them to salvation, not wrath. And verse 10 is one of the earliest written statements of why Jesus died: ‘He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him.’ Here ‘awake or asleep’ seems to mean alive or dead, picking up the word sleep from chapter 4. Whether they are living or have died when he comes, they will live with him.

And once again, Paul ends with a task for all of them: encourage and build one another up. Everyone has a part.
passages.ot:
The armour comes from Isaiah, where God himself prepares to act: “He put on righteousness like a breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head” (Isaiah 59:17). Paul gives God's own armour to his people.

Light and darkness run through the prophets. “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2). “Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you” (Isaiah 60:1).

And Proverbs paints the drunkard of the night: “When can I wake up to search for another drink?” (Proverbs 23:35).
passages.asks: Paul tells the church to stay awake and sober, and to put on faith, love and hope. Ask where you have fallen asleep to God, drifting through days without thinking of him. Ask which piece of the armour you most need to put on this week. And ask whom you could encourage and build up, as Paul says they were already doing.

passages.t: Honour your leaders, and care for everyone
passages.happening:
“But we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who preside over you in the Lord and give you instruction. In love, hold them in highest regard because of their work. Live in peace with one another” (verses 12-13).

“And we urge you, brothers, to admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone. Make sure that no one repays evil for evil. Always pursue what is good for one another and for all people” (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
Only months after it began, the church already had leaders. Paul does not give them titles; the words ‘elder’ and ‘overseer’ are not used here. He describes them by what they do. They ‘work diligently’, the same word for tiring toil Paul used of his own work. They ‘preside’, which means to stand at the head and lead. And they ‘give instruction’, which can mean to warn. Paul asks the church to honour them ‘because of their work’, not because of their rank.

Then he turns to everyone. The care of the church is not only the leaders' job. Each of the four commands fits a different need. The ‘unruly’ are those out of line; the word was used of soldiers out of step, and here it likely includes those who had stopped working (4:11). They need a warning. The ‘fainthearted’ are the discouraged and anxious, perhaps those grieving their dead. They need encouragement, not a lecture. The ‘weak’ may be those weak in faith or weak in body; either way they need someone to hold on to them. And ‘everyone’ needs patience.

Notice that Paul does not say ‘admonish everyone’. A wise church tells the difference between someone who will not and someone who cannot.

And then: no revenge. These believers were being mistreated by their neighbours. Paul tells them not to pay back evil, and to pursue what is good ‘for all people’, including those neighbours.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament asks shepherds to care for every kind of sheep. God condemned leaders who did not: “You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured” (Ezekiel 34:4). And he promised to do it himself: “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16).

Refusing revenge is in the law and the wisdom books. “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). “Do not say, ‘I will avenge this evil!’ Wait on the LORD, and He will save you” (Proverbs 20:22). And Proverbs goes further: “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat” (Proverbs 25:21).
passages.hard:
Does ‘hold them in highest regard’ mean that church leaders must never be questioned?

No. Paul asks the church to honour leaders ‘because of their work’, the hard, caring work of those who serve. He gives no leader a right to control people, to demand silence, or to escape being questioned. In the same breath he tells the whole church to care for the weak and to ‘live in peace with one another’. Christians agree that leaders are servants accountable to Christ and to his word, and that no authority may be used to cover abuse.

If a leader uses his place to control, exploit or harm, these verses do not protect him. Anyone harmed by a church leader is free to speak to another trusted leader, a counselor, or, where a crime is involved, the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul names four kinds of people a church must care for: the unruly, the fainthearted, the weak, and everyone. Ask which of them you are right now, and who has cared for you. Ask whether you have mistaken someone who cannot for someone who will not. And ask whether there is anyone you are quietly paying back for a wrong.

passages.t: Rejoice, pray, give thanks; test everything
passages.happening:
Paul gives a string of short commands. “Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus” (verses 16-18).

“Do not extinguish the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things. Hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every form of evil” (verses 19-22).
passages.hearers:
Some of these commands are only two or three words in Greek. They read almost like a rule of life for a church.

‘Pray without ceasing’ does not mean doing nothing but pray. The word means something that keeps coming back, again and again, without giving up. Paul used the same word of his own prayers for them (1:3; 2:13). It describes a life where prayer is always returning, like breathing.

‘Give thanks in every circumstance’ says ‘in’, not ‘for’. Paul does not ask anyone to be thankful for evil. He asks them to find, even in a hard place, that God is still good and still near. He was writing to a church that was suffering, from a man who was suffering too.

Then Paul turns to the Spirit's gifts. To ‘extinguish’ the Spirit is to put out a fire. In the early churches some believers prophesied, speaking a word they believed came from God for the church. Some in Thessalonica may have grown wary of it. Paul says do not despise it, and do not swallow it whole either: ‘test all things’. Keep what is good. Throw away every form of evil. The picture behind ‘test’ is of testing coins or metal to see whether they are real.
passages.ot:
Joy in hard times has deep roots in the Old Testament. Habakkuk said that though the crops fail and the stalls are empty, “yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation” (Habakkuk 3:18). David said, “I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise will always be on my lips” (Psalm 34:1).

Daniel prayed and gave thanks three times a day, “just as he had done before”, even when it was against the law (Daniel 6:10).

Moses wished for the Spirit on everyone: “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them” (Numbers 11:29). Yet the law also told Israel to test a prophet's word: “When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken” (Deuteronomy 18:22).
passages.hard:
Does ‘Rejoice at all times’ mean a Christian should never be sad? And does prophecy still happen?

Rejoicing at all times is not pretending. Paul wept, worried and grieved, and said so in his letters. Joy in Christ can sit beside sorrow without cancelling it. ‘Give thanks in every circumstance’ is never a reason to tell someone who has been hurt that the harm was really good for them.

If sadness has settled on you and will not lift, these verses do not shame you. When grief or sadness lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise, and it is not a failure of faith. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone now: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

On prophecy, Christians differ. Some believe the gift of prophecy continues in the church today. Others believe it ended with the apostles, and that God now speaks through the finished Scriptures. Others take a middle way. These notes do not choose. All can take Paul's pattern: do not despise what God may be doing, and test everything by his word.
passages.asks: Paul asks for joy, prayer and thanks in every circumstance. Ask what you could thank God for today, even in what is hard. Ask whether your prayer is something you do now and then, or something that keeps coming back. And ask whether you test what you hear, from preachers, online or in your own heart, before you hold on to it.

passages.t: The God of peace will make you holy
passages.happening:
“Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it” (verses 23-24).

“Brothers, pray for us as well. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you” (verses 25-28).
passages.hearers:
The letter ends where the first half ended (3:13), with a prayer for holiness at the coming of the Lord. But the weight falls on God. It is ‘the God of peace Himself’ who will make them holy, and ‘completely’. And then the promise: ‘The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it.’ Their holiness does not depend on their strength. It depends on his faithfulness.

‘Spirit, soul, and body’ means the whole person, every part. Some Christians read these words as teaching that a person has three distinct parts. Others read them as Paul's way of saying ‘all of you’, since elsewhere Scripture speaks of a person as body and soul. Either way, the body is included. God's holiness reaches all the way down.

Paul asks them to pray for him. The great apostle needs the prayers of a church only months old.

The ‘holy kiss’ was a common greeting among family and friends in that world. Christians used it as a sign that fellow believers were family.

And Paul charges them solemnly to have the letter read ‘to all the brothers’. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church, so that everyone heard them together. Paul wants no one left out.
passages.ot:
God is the faithful one: “Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations” (Deuteronomy 7:9).

The God of peace keeps his people: “You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You” (Isaiah 26:3).

And Paul's last words of grace echo the old priestly blessing, which ends, “the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26).
passages.asks: Paul ends with a promise: the One who calls you is faithful, and he will do it. Ask where you have been trying to make yourself holy by your own strength. Ask whom you could ask to pray for you, as Paul did. And ask whether there is anyone in your church who is being left out, whom you could greet as family.
